claims.text: The alloy has an equimolar W-Ta-Ti-V-Zr composition.
The controlled comparison can match the alloy and pure tungsten in grain structure, porosity, and thermal and mechanical history.
Temperatures of approximately 800–1200°C are representative of high-temperature plasma-facing-component service.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has a BCC matrix under the proposed test conditions.
The multi-principal-element composition produces lattice distortion within the BCC matrix.
The multi-principal-element composition creates heterogeneous local atomic environments.
Lattice distortion and solid-solution effects create heterogeneous obstacles to dislocation motion.
These heterogeneous obstacles create spatially variable atomic-scale resistance to dislocation motion.
The modified dislocation behavior enhances energy dissipation during deformation.
Enhanced energy dissipation delays crack initiation and propagation.
Delayed crack initiation and propagation improve ductility and fracture toughness relative to pure tungsten.
At 800–1200°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain than matched commercially pure tungsten.
At 800–1200°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater fracture toughness and crack-propagation resistance than matched commercially pure tungsten.
Commercially pure tungsten has limited ductility and lower fracture toughness at elevated temperatures.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to single-phase microstructures at approximately 800–1200°C.
Extensive secondary-phase formation or grain coarsening may limit the validity of the proposed mechanism.
Grain-boundary modifications or secondary phases may also contribute to the mechanical response.
Matched high-temperature tensile and fracture-toughness tests, combined with post-deformation TEM, can test the proposed composition–lattice-distortion–dislocation mechanism.
